:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac {3} {x} y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}, \qquad x \gt 0.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = x^3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm d x = uv - \int u' v\,\textrm d x
$$

Let $u = x, u' = 1, v' = \cos x,$ and $v = \sin x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}y) & ={x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2}) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int {u}^{′}v\,\text{d}x
$$

Let $u=x,{u}^{′}=1,{v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and $v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{2} & =\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =x(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{2} & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,+C \\ y & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{x}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}},\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{{e}^{x}}{{x}^{3}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{3})\,dx & =\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & ={e}^{x}+C \\ y & =\frac{{e}^{x}+C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y=7,\,x>0.
$$

Select the correct options below:

$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{5}{x}$ and $Q(x)=7.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int (5/x)\,dx} \\  & ={e}^{5\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5})} \\  & ={x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={x}^{5}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{5}{x}y) & ={x}^{5}\cdot 7 \\ {x}^{5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+5{x}^{4}y & =7{x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(y{x}^{5})\,dx & =\int 7{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{5} & =\frac{7{x}^{6}}{6}+C \\ y & =\frac{7x}{6}+\frac{C}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=6{e}^{2x}.
$$

Select the correct options below.$\,$ An integrating factor for this equation is $I(x)=$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The general solution is given by $y(x)=$ {{field-2}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is already in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=-3$ and $Q(x)=6{e}^{2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int -3\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)={e}^{-3x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y) & ={e}^{-3x}\cdot 6{e}^{2x} \\ {e}^{-3x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{e}^{-3x}\cdot y & =6{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x))$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x}) & =6{e}^{-x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{-3x})\text{d}x & =\int 6{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{-3x} & =-6{e}^{-x}+C \\ y & =-6{e}^{2x}+C{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x),
$$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot 9{x}^{2} \\ {e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot y & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}}) & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3+C{e}^{-{0}^{3}} \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y = 3 - 2e^{-x^3}.
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Recall that a first-order linear ODE can always be expressed in the standard form

$$
y'(x)+P(x)y(x) =Q(x).
$$

First-order linear ODEs are special because we can always find the general solution using an **integrating factor.** 

An integrating factor is a function $I(x)$ that allows us to rewrite the left-hand side as an exact derivative after multiplying the equation by $I(x).$ The resulting equation can then be solved by integrating both sides.

To demonstrate, consider the following first-order linear ODE.

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + \frac{2}{x}\, y = 3
$$

As it stands, this differential equation cannot be integrated directly. However, if we multiply both sides of the equation by $I(x) = x^2,$ we get

$$
x^2\cdot \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + x^2\cdot \frac{2}{x}\, y = x^2\cdot 3
$$

which simplifies as follows:

$$
x^2 \frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + 2 x y = 3x^2 \qquad (\ast)
$$

Now, here's the neat part. Provided our integrating factor is correct, we can *always* write the left-hand side of the equation as the exact derivative

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)
$$

which in our case is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(y \cdot x^2\right).
$$

So, our differential equation is

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}( y \cdot x^2) = 3x^2.
$$

We can now find the general solution by integrating both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot {x}^{2}) & =3{x}^{2} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot {x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ y\cdot {x}^{2} & ={x}^{3}+C \\ y=x+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We can check that 

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}( y \cdot x^2) = 3x^2
$$

is indeed equivalent to the original equation $(\ast)$ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot {x}^{2}) & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y)\cdot {x}^{2}+y\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =3{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\cdot 2x & =3{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy & =3{x}^{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

By finding an appropriate integrating factor, we can solve any first-order linear ODE! So the question is, how do we find an integrating factor? Let's discuss this next.

Given a first-order linear ODE, we can find an integrating factor and use it to solve the equation using the following procedure.

- **Step 1**: Write the equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

- **Step 2**: Compute an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition

$$
I(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,\textrm{d}x} \,.
$$

- **Step 3**: Multiply both sides of the equation found in step 1 by $I(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + I(x)P(x)y = I(x)Q(x)
$$

- **Step 4**: Rewrite the left side as 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y I(x)\Bigr)
$$

If steps 1 through 3 are done correctly, then we can always do this, and we can check that it's correct by differentiating. Our new equation is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y I(x)\Bigr) = I(x)Q(x)
$$

- **Step 5**: Integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x$ and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))\,\text{d}x & =\int I(x)Q(x)\,\text{d}x \\ yI(x) & =\int I(x)Q(x)\,\text{d}x+C \\ y & =\frac{1}{I(x)}(\int I(x)Q(x)\,\text{d}x+C)\end{aligned}
$$

You might be wondering where the formula for $I(x)$ comes from; we'll discuss this at the end of the lesson. First, let's apply this method to a concrete example in the next slide.

$$

with $P(x) = 3x^2$ and $Q(x) = 9x^2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We will now derive the formula for the integrating factor. 

Consider the first-order linear equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x).
$$

Our goal is to rewrite the left-hand side as the derivative of a product.

To do that, we multiply both sides of the equation by some function $I(x)$ that we wish to determine.

$$
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I(x)P(x)}y} = I(x)Q(x)
$$

We want the left-hand side to match the derivative of $y\cdot I(x)$. But by the product rule,

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr)
=
{\color{blue}I(x)\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + {\color{purple}I'(x)}y}.
$$

So, if we choose $I(x)$ so that

$$
I'(x) = I(x)P(x),
$$

then the left-hand side becomes $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Bigl(y\cdot I(x)\Bigr).$

Dividing both sides of $I'(x) = I(x)P(x)$ by $I(x)$ gives

$$
\frac{I'(x)}{I(x)} = P(x).
$$

Next, integrating both sides with respect to $x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{I}^{′}(x)}{I(x)}\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)))\,\text{d}x & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(I(x)) & =\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C \\ I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x+C} \\  & ={e}^{C}\cdot {e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, because multiplying $I(x)$ by a nonzero constant does not change the method, we can choose $e^C = 1$ and define an integrating factor as

$$
I(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,\textrm{d}x}.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x) - 3\sin(2x) = 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
f'(x) = 3\sin{2x}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} = x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{6}{x}^{3}+Cx+D\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$ We cannot combine them, because $C$ is being multiplied by $x$ while $D$ is not.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $f(0)=2.$

$$
f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0) = 2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ 2 & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is 

$$
f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int uv' \, \textrm{d}x= uv - \int vu' \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle  \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle  \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{7x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}-\int \frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{7}\int {e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{7}\left(\frac{{e}^{7x}}{7}\right)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{49}{e}^{7x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle \int x \cos{2x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\cdot \frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\int (-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x))\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\frac{1}{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)|}_{0}^{\pi /5}+{\frac{1}{5}\left(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)}{5}\right)|}_{0}^{\pi /5} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{5}\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\frac{1}{5}\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)]+[\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[-\frac{\pi }{25}\cdot (-1)+0]+[0-0] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{25}.\end{aligned}
$$
